title: CCNA 200-301 (v2.0) practice exam

domains.name: AI, and Network Operations and Management

note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from Cisco's public 200-301 CCNA v2.0 exam topics (testing starts Feb 3, 2027). Not real exam questions. Cisco doesn't publish the number of items; this is a 100-item stand-in in 120 minutes with 4 drag-and-drop style items. The real CCNA can also include hands-on labs.

q.q: Users on SW1 Gi1/0/5 say file copies crawl. The other end of the link is set to 100 Mb/s full duplex. What is the problem?
o: A duplex mismatch
Right. Late collisions on the half-duplex side are the classic sign. Set both ends the same, ideally auto.
A bad cable causing CRC errors
The output shows 0 CRC errors.
The port is in the wrong VLAN
A VLAN problem would stop traffic, not slow it with collisions.
The link is over 100 meters
Distance problems show up as CRC errors and link drops.
q.code:
SW1#show interfaces gi1/0/5
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  ...
  0 input errors, 0 CRC
  1873 late collision, 0 deferred

q.q: A full-duplex gigabit port shows input errors and CRC errors climbing every minute, but no collisions. What should you check FIRST?
o: The cable and connectors
Right. CRC errors on a full-duplex link usually point to a physical problem like a bad cable, a bad connector or EMI.
The duplex setting
Full duplex has no collisions, and nothing here points to a mismatch.
The VLAN on the port
VLANs don't cause CRC errors.
Which switch is the spanning tree root bridge
STP doesn't corrupt frames.

q.q: A new 1000BASE-T copper run from the switch to a far office measures 135 m. The link flaps and logs errors. What is the cause?
o: It's past the 100 m copper limit
Right. Copper Ethernet is rated to 100 m. Use fiber or add a switch in the middle.
1000BASE-T needs single-mode fiber
1000BASE-T is copper.
The port needs PoE turned off
PoE doesn't cause errors from distance.
Gigabit copper links must always use a crossover cable
Gigabit ports handle cable type with Auto-MDIX.

q.q: A 10 km fiber link between buildings won't come up. Optics output shows Rx power at -27 dBm, below the -14 dBm low alarm. The SFPs are 1000BASE-SX. What is the MOST likely problem?
o: SX optics can't reach 10 km
Right. 1000BASE-SX reaches only a few hundred meters. A 10 km run needs long-reach optics such as LX/LH on single-mode fiber.
The switch needs a higher MTU
MTU doesn't affect light levels.
The duplex is set to half
Fiber gigabit links are full duplex. The light level is the issue.
The VLAN isn't allowed on the trunk between the buildings
A VLAN issue wouldn't lower receive power.

q.q: Two older switches with Auto-MDIX turned off are connected with a straight-through cable. The ports stay down. What fixes it?
o: Crossover cable or Auto-MDIX
Right. Like devices need a crossover cable unless Auto-MDIX swaps the pairs.
Hard-set both ports to half duplex and 100 Mb/s
Duplex doesn't fix a pinout problem.
Change the native VLAN
VLANs don't bring up a dead link.
Turn on PortFast
PortFast skips STP delays. It doesn't fix cabling.

q.q: Which hypervisor runs directly on the server hardware with no host operating system under it?
o: Type 1 (bare metal), like VMware ESXi
Right. Type 1 hypervisors are the OS on the hardware.
Type 2, like VirtualBox on Windows
Type 2 runs as an app on top of a host OS.
A container runtime, like Docker
Container runtimes run on a host OS and don't create VMs.
A virtual switch
A virtual switch connects VMs. It isn't a hypervisor.

q.q: Compared with virtual machines, why do containers start faster and use less memory?
o: They share the host's kernel
Right. A container packages the app and its libraries, not a whole guest OS.
They run on dedicated hardware
Containers run on shared hosts.
They skip the network stack
Containers still use networking.
They always run on a Type 1 hypervisor under the hood
Containers don't need a hypervisor.

q.q: One physical server must run a Windows Server app and a Linux app side by side, each with its own OS. What fits BEST?
o: Two VMs on a hypervisor
Right. Each VM has its own kernel, so Windows and Linux can run side by side.
Two Linux containers on one host
Linux containers share a Linux kernel, so they can't run a Windows app natively.
One container with both apps
A container can't hold two different kernels.
A Layer 3 switch with two VRFs
VRFs split routing tables. They don't run apps.

q.q: An ESXi host carries VMs in VLANs 10 and 20 over one physical NIC to switch port Gi1/0/12. How should Gi1/0/12 be set?
o: An 802.1Q trunk for VLANs 10 and 20
Right. The host's virtual switch tags the frames, so the switch port must accept both VLANs.
As an access port in VLAN 10
An access port carries one VLAN, so VLAN 20 would fail.
As a routed port with no switchport
A routed port doesn't carry VLANs.
Shut down, because ESXi needs a separate NIC per VLAN
One NIC can carry several VLANs on a trunk.

q.q: What connects VMs on the same host to each other and to the physical network?
o: A virtual switch in the hypervisor
Right. The vSwitch forwards frames between VMs and out the physical NICs.
A container image
An image is a package for a container.
The guest OS kernel
Each VM's kernel runs inside the VM, not between VMs.
A WLAN controller on the management network
A WLC manages access points.

q.q: A PC is set to 192.168.10.77/27 with gateway 192.168.10.97. It reaches local hosts but nothing off the subnet. Why?
o: The gateway is in another subnet
Right. 192.168.10.77/27 is in 64-95. The gateway .97 is in 96-127, so the PC can't reach it.
The PC's address is a broadcast address
The broadcast for that subnet is .95.
/27 masks can't use a gateway
Any subnet can use a gateway.
192.168.10.0 isn't part of any private address range
It's in the 192.168.0.0/16 private range.

q.q: You must cut 10.1.0.0/24 into subnets of at least 50 hosts each and want as many subnets as possible. Which mask?
o: Right. /26 gives 62 usable hosts, the smallest size that fits 50.
/25 fits 126 hosts, but you get fewer subnets.
/27 gives only 30 usable hosts.
/24 gives one subnet.

q.q: What is the broadcast address for host 172.16.5.200/23?
o: Right. /23 blocks go in 2s in the third octet: 172.16.4.0 to 172.16.5.255.
That's inside the block, not its end.
That's a host inside the /23.
That belongs to the next block.

q.q: Which address is NOT a private RFC 1918 address?
o: Right. The private range is 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so 172.32 is public.
10.0.0.0/8 is private.

q.q: A server is set to 10.10.10.64/26 and can't talk to anything. What is wrong with the address?
o: It's the network ID of 10.10.10.64/26
Right. 10.10.10.64/26 covers 64-127, and .64 is the network ID, not a usable host.
It's a public address
10.0.0.0/8 is private.
A /26 is too small a subnet for a server to use
Mask size doesn't stop one host from working.
It's the broadcast address
The broadcast is .127.

q.q: With prefix 2001:db8:1:1::/64 and MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E, what EUI-64 address does the interface build?
o: Right. Split the MAC, insert FFFE, and flip the 7th bit of the first byte (00 becomes 02).
This forgets to flip the 7th bit, which makes 00 into 02.
FFFE goes in the middle of the MAC, not the end.
FFFE goes between the two MAC halves.

q.q: Every IPv6-enabled interface gets an address starting with FE80. What type is it, and how far does it reach?
o: Link-local, valid only on that link
Right. FE80::/10 addresses are never routed.
Global unicast, routed on the internet
Global unicast is 2000::/3.
Unique local, routed only inside the company
Unique local is FC00::/7.
Multicast to all routers
Multicast starts with FF.

q.q: Which is a valid short form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329?
o: Right. Drop leading zeros in each group and replace one run of zero groups with ::.
:: can only appear once.
That has only seven groups, so a zero group is missing.
Leading zeros can go, but ff00 can't become ff.

q.q: Your site gets a /48 from the ISP. Each LAN gets a /64. How many /64 subnets can you make?
o: Right. 64 minus 48 is 16 bits, and 2 to the 16th is 65,536.
That would be 8 bits, a /56.
16 is the number of bits, not subnets.
That would be 12 bits.

q.q: An internal IPv6 network should never be reachable from the internet, like RFC 1918 space. Which prefix fits?
o: Unique local, FD00::/8
Right. Unique local addresses (FC00::/7, FD00::/8 in practice) are for private use.
Link-local, FE80::/10
Link-local can't be routed between your own subnets.
Global unicast, 2000::/3
That's internet-routable space.
Multicast, FF00::/8
Multicast isn't used for host addressing.

q.q: You're planning 2.4 GHz access points next to each other in North America. Which channels avoid overlap?
o: Right. These three 20 MHz channels don't overlap in the 2.4 GHz band.
1, 2 and 3
These are next to each other and overlap badly.
Those are 5 GHz channels.
13 isn't used in North America.

q.q: Why do 5 GHz networks often perform better than 2.4 GHz in a busy office, even though the range is shorter?
o: More channels, less interference
Right. More channels mean less overlap. 2.4 GHz is shared with microwaves and Bluetooth.
5 GHz passes through walls and floors better than 2.4 GHz
Higher frequencies lose more through walls.
5 GHz doesn't need encryption
Both bands need encryption.
5 GHz uses a wider SSID
SSIDs don't have a width.

q.q: What does WPA3-Personal use to stop offline password-guessing attacks on a captured handshake?
o: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)
Right. SAE replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key exchange and resists offline dictionary attacks.
TKIP
TKIP is the old WPA cipher and is deprecated.
WEP keys
WEP is broken and obsolete.
Open authentication
Open networks have no password at all.

q.q: Wi-Fi in the break room drops every day around noon on 2.4 GHz only. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: A microwave oven in the break room
Right. Microwave ovens leak energy near 2.4 GHz.
The 5 GHz radio being turned off
The problem is on 2.4 GHz.
DHCP lease times
DHCP doesn't depend on lunchtime.
Too many SSIDs broadcast on the 5 GHz radio
The drop is only on 2.4 GHz.

q.q: A laptop shows RSSI -82 dBm with a noise floor of -90 dBm. What can you conclude?
o: The SNR is only 8 dB, too low for a reliable link
Right. Signal minus noise is 8 dB. Most data needs about 20 dB or more.
The signal is excellent, because -82 is a large number
In dBm, closer to zero is stronger. -82 is weak.
The SNR is 172 dB
You subtract the values, you don't add them.
The noise is louder than the signal
-90 is weaker than -82, so the signal is still above the noise.

q.q: A Windows PC shows this. What does the address tell you?
o: The PC got no DHCP reply
Right. 169.254.x.x is APIPA, which Windows assigns itself when DHCP fails.
DHCP worked and handed out a private address
169.254 is self-assigned, not handed out by DHCP.
The PC has a static address
APIPA means DHCP was tried and failed.
The DNS server is down
DNS doesn't hand out addresses.
q.code:
C:\>ipconfig
  IPv4 Address. . . : 169.254.33.10
  Subnet Mask . . . : 255.255.0.0
  Default Gateway . :

q.q: A Linux server can ping hosts on its own subnet but nothing else. Which output explains it?
o: ip route shows no 'default via' line
Right. With no default route, the server only reaches directly connected subnets.
ip addr shows its own address with /24
That's a normal subnet setting.
The DNS resolver file lists two servers
DNS doesn't affect pinging by IP.
ip link shows the interface UP
UP is good, not the problem.

q.q: From a Mac, ping 8.8.8.8 works but ping www.cisco.com fails with 'cannot resolve'. What should you check?
o: The DNS server setting
Right. Reaching IPs but not names points to name resolution.
The default gateway
The gateway works, because 8.8.8.8 replied.
The Wi-Fi password saved on the Mac
The Mac is already connected.
The subnet mask
Off-subnet pings work, so the mask is fine.

q.q: A PC is set to 192.168.1.50 with mask 255.255.0.0 and a correct gateway. The real LAN is a /24. It can't reach 192.168.2.10 on another subnet. Why?
o: The PC thinks the host is local
Right. With the wrong mask, the PC never sends that traffic to its gateway.
The gateway blocks /16 hosts
Gateways don't check a host's mask.
192.168.2.10 isn't a private address
It's private.
The PC needs IPv6 turned on to reach other subnets
IPv4 routing works fine with the right mask.

q.q: The office switched its Wi-Fi to WPA3-only. Most laptops connect, but an older scanner that supports only WPA2 can't. What is the BEST fix while you replace it?
o: Transition mode or a WPA2 SSID
Right. Transition mode accepts both WPA2 and WPA3 clients. A separate SSID keeps the exception small.
Turn off encryption on the main SSID
An open network would expose everyone.
Switch the main SSID to WEP
WEP is broken.
Give the scanner a static IP address and DNS server
Addressing doesn't fix a security mismatch.

q.q: Clients in VLAN 20 get no addresses. The DHCP server is at 10.0.0.5 in another subnet. What is missing on the VLAN 20 SVI?
o: ip helper-address 10.0.0.5
Right. The helper turns broadcast DHCP requests into unicast sent to the server.
ip dhcp snooping trust
Snooping trust goes on switch ports, not as a relay.
ip address dhcp
That makes the SVI a DHCP client.
service dhcp disable
That turns DHCP services off.

q.q: What is the correct order of the four DHCPv4 messages when a client first gets an address?
o: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
Right. DORA.
Request, Offer, Discover, Acknowledge
The client discovers servers first.
Discover, Request, Offer, Acknowledge
The server offers before the client requests.
Offer, Discover, Acknowledge, Request
The client starts the exchange.

q.q: An IOS DHCP pool for 192.168.1.0/24 hands out 192.168.1.1, which is the router's own address, causing conflicts. What fixes it?
o: ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.10
Right. Excluded addresses are never leased.
default-router 192.168.1.1
That tells clients the gateway. It doesn't stop leasing it.
lease 0 1
Lease time doesn't exclude addresses.
no ip dhcp conflict logging
That hides conflicts. It doesn't fix them.

q.q: The ISP hands your router its WAN address by DHCP. Which command goes on the WAN interface?
o: ip address dhcp
Right. This makes the interface a DHCP client.
ip helper-address dhcp
Helper needs a server address and relays for clients.
ip dhcp pool WAN
That creates a local pool for clients.
ip dhcp client enable
That isn't the IOS command.

q.q: Which command shows the addresses an IOS router's DHCP server has leased, with each client's MAC?
o: show ip dhcp binding
Right. It lists leased IPs, client IDs and lease expiry.
show ip dhcp pool
This shows pool settings and usage counts, not each client.
show ip interface brief
This shows interface addresses.
show arp
ARP shows MACs of hosts it has talked to, not DHCP leases.

q.q: SW1 logs this message every minute. What is the effect?
o: Untagged traffic leaks between VLANs
Right. Each side treats untagged traffic as its own native VLAN, so VLAN 1 and VLAN 99 traffic leak into each other.
The trunk shuts down
A native VLAN mismatch doesn't shut the trunk.
Every tagged VLAN on the trunk stops forwarding
Tagged VLANs keep working.
CDP turns off on both switches
CDP is what reported it.
q.code:
%CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch
 discovered on GigabitEthernet1/0/24 (1),
 with SW2 GigabitEthernet1/0/24 (99).

q.q: A trunk carried VLANs 10 and 20. An engineer typed the command below to add VLAN 30. Now VLANs 10 and 20 are down across the trunk. Why?
o: It replaced the whole allowed list
Right. Without the add keyword, the list is overwritten. Use switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30.
VLAN 30 now has a higher priority than VLANs 10 and 20
VLANs don't have priorities on a trunk.
Trunks can only carry two VLANs
Trunks can carry thousands of VLANs.
The native VLAN changed to 30
This command doesn't touch the native VLAN.

q.q: Two switches are cabled with four links for an LACP EtherChannel. Which mode pair will NOT form a channel?
o: passive on both sides
Right. Passive only answers LACP. If neither side starts, no channel forms.
active on both sides
Both send LACP, so the channel forms.
active on one side, passive on the other
The active side starts, and the passive side answers.
active on one side, active on the other after a reload
Active-active forms no matter when it's set.

q.q: show etherchannel summary shows Po1(SU) with Gi1/0/1(P) and Gi1/0/2(s). What is the MOST likely reason Gi1/0/2 is suspended?
o: Its settings don't match the bundle
Right. Members must match. A mismatched port is suspended so it can't cause a loop.
It's the hot-standby member, so it waits for Gi1/0/1 to fail
LACP bundles all matching ports. Suspended isn't standby.
The port-channel is a Layer 3 interface
The S flag shows Po1 is Layer 2.
STP put it in forwarding
STP treats the bundle as one link.

q.q: On a Layer 3 switch, SVIs for VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 are up/up with IP addresses, but hosts in VLAN 10 can't reach VLAN 20. Which global command is likely missing?
o: ip routing
Right. Without ip routing, a Layer 3 switch won't route between its SVIs.
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
STP mode doesn't enable routing.
vtp mode transparent
VTP mode doesn't route traffic.
no switchport
That makes a physical port routed. The SVIs already exist.

q.q: A router connects to a switch trunk to route VLANs 10 and 20 (router on a stick). Which config is right for VLAN 10 on the router?
o: This config, with the switch port set as a trunk
Right. Each subinterface tags one VLAN and acts as that VLAN's gateway.
This config, with the switch port in access VLAN 10
An access port can't carry VLAN 20 too.
The subinterface needs switchport mode trunk
Routers don't use switchport commands.
The physical Gi0/0/1 needs the VLAN 10 address
The address goes on the subinterface.
q.code:
interface Gi0/0/1.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0

q.q: Both ends of a link are set to switchport mode dynamic auto. What does the link become?
o: An access port
Right. Dynamic auto waits for the other side to ask. If both wait, no trunk forms.
A trunk
A trunk needs at least one side to be desirable or trunk.
An EtherChannel
DTP doesn't build EtherChannels.
A routed port
DTP doesn't make routed ports.

q.q: A desk has an IP phone, with a PC plugged into the phone. Voice must use VLAN 20 and the PC VLAN 10. Which port config fits?
o: This config
Right. The phone tags voice in VLAN 20, and the PC's untagged traffic goes to access VLAN 10.
The same, but with switchport mode trunk and native VLAN 20
Voice VLAN is the normal setup, and voice shouldn't be the native VLAN.
switchport access vlan 20 only
The PC would land in the voice VLAN.
Two ports, one per device
The phone's built-in switch lets one port serve both.
q.code:
interface Gi1/0/8
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport voice vlan 20

q.q: An autonomous AP serves two SSIDs: STAFF in VLAN 10 and GUEST in VLAN 30. How should its switch port be set?
o: A trunk carrying VLANs 10 and 30
Right. A standalone AP puts each SSID's traffic on its own VLAN, so the port needs both.
As an access port in VLAN 10
GUEST traffic would have nowhere to go.
As a routed port with an IP in each VLAN
The AP bridges SSIDs to VLANs. It doesn't route.
As an access port in VLAN 30
STAFF would end up in the guest VLAN.

q.q: A lightweight AP in local mode joins a WLC that switches all client traffic centrally. How is its switch port USUALLY set?
o: An access port in the AP's VLAN
Right. In local mode, client traffic rides the CAPWAP tunnel to the WLC, so the AP port needs only one VLAN.
As a trunk with every client VLAN
That's what FlexConnect local switching or an autonomous AP needs.
As a routed port running OSPF to the WLC
APs don't run OSPF.
As an EtherChannel to the WLC
The AP connects to an access switch, not to the WLC directly.

q.q: A new Wi-Fi 6 AP boots, then keeps rebooting. Look at the output. What is the MOST likely problem?
o: The switch's PoE budget is used up
Right. A class 4 device needs up to 30 W (PoE+), but only 15.4 W was given and the budget is nearly gone.
The AP needs a crossover cable to draw full power
Auto-MDIX handles this, and the port is up.
The port is in the wrong VLAN
A VLAN problem wouldn't make it reboot.
PoE is turned off on the port
Admin is auto and Oper is on.
q.code:
SW1#show power inline gi1/0/14
Interface Admin Oper  Power  Device   Class
Gi1/0/14  auto  on    15.4   AIR-AP   4
SW1#show power inline
Available:370.0(w) Used:368.2(w) Remaining:1.8(w)

q.q: A virtualization host bonds two NICs with LACP to switch ports Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/2. What must the switch side have?
o: Both in channel-group 1 mode active
Right. The switch must bundle the same ports with LACP so the host's team works.
Each port in a different VLAN
Bundled ports must match.
PortFast and BPDU guard on each port, with no channel
Those don't bundle the links.
channel-group 1 mode on at one end, passive at the other
On doesn't speak LACP, so it can't pair with passive.

q.q: At boot, PCs get 169.254 addresses, but after a minute they work. The ports are plain access ports. What fixes it?
o: Turn on PortFast
Right. Without PortFast, the port waits through STP states before forwarding, and the PC's DHCP times out.
Turn off DHCP snooping
Snooping doesn't delay a port coming up.
Set the ports to trunk
Trunks still go through STP.
Lower the DHCP lease time to one hour
Lease time doesn't affect the first request.

q.q: IoT sensors should be kept apart from office PCs on the same access switches. What is the simplest step at the edge?
o: Put the sensors in their own VLAN
Right. A separate VLAN keeps them in their own subnet, where ACLs or a firewall can control access.
Make every sensor port a trunk
Trunks don't isolate anything.
Turn off CDP and LLDP on all the sensor ports
CDP doesn't separate traffic.
Give each sensor a public IP address
That makes them more exposed.

q.q: A firewall pair connects to two stacked switches and needs both links active with failover. What should the switch ports use?
o: A cross-stack LACP trunk
Right. A cross-stack port channel gives two active links and survives losing one switch.
Two separate access ports in different VLANs
That doesn't give one logical link with failover.
Two access ports with STP blocking one
STP would block one link, so they aren't both active.
A single routed port on the first stack member
One port has no redundancy.

q.q: The diagram says SW1 Gi1/0/24 goes to R1 Gi0/0/1. Look at the output. What is TRUE?
o: R1 is really on SW1 port Gi1/0/23
Right. Local Intrfce is the switch port. Port ID is R1's port.
R1's own port is Gi1/0/23
Port ID shows R1's port: Gig 0/0/1.
CDP can't be trusted for cabling
CDP is a standard way to check cabling.
The 152-second holdtime shows the link is going down
Holdtime counts down between CDP updates.
q.code:
SW1#show cdp neighbors
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Capability  Platform  Port ID
R1         Gig 1/0/23     152      R I         ISR4331   Gig 0/0/1

q.q: show cdp neighbors on a Cisco switch doesn't list the third-party switch on Gi1/0/48. What should you use?
o: LLDP, with lldp run
Right. LLDP is the open standard most vendors support. CDP is Cisco's own.
show mac address-table only
That shows MACs, not which device or port.
VTP
VTP shares VLANs. It doesn't discover neighbors.
Change the port to a trunk
Port mode doesn't make CDP work with other vendors.

q.q: You need the management IP address and software version of a directly connected Cisco router. Which command shows them?
o: show cdp neighbors detail
Right. The detail view lists the IP address, platform and IOS version.
show cdp neighbors
The summary doesn't include IP addresses.
show ip interface brief
That shows your own interfaces.
show lldp neighbors on the router
That shows whether LLDP is on, not neighbor details.

q.q: LLDP is on in global config, but one access port toward a printer shows no LLDP neighbor. The printer supports LLDP. What is a likely cause?
o: LLDP is turned off on that one port
Right. Ports can have no lldp transmit or no lldp receive set.
LLDP only works on trunk ports
LLDP works on access ports.
The port needs CDP turned off first
CDP and LLDP can run together.
Printers need an IP address in VLAN 1 to send LLDP
LLDP works at Layer 2, with no IP needed.

q.q: Why do many teams turn off CDP on internet-facing interfaces?
o: It reveals device models and versions
Right. That information helps attackers plan.
CDP uses too much bandwidth
CDP traffic is tiny.
CDP stops routing protocols like OSPF from working on that link
It doesn't affect routing.
CDP only works on internal VLANs
It works on any Cisco link.

q.q: Two routers on one link have IPs in different subnets and can't ping each other, but each sees the other in show cdp neighbors. Why does CDP still work?
o: CDP works at Layer 2, without IP
Right. CDP frames go between neighbors whatever their IP settings.
CDP routes between subnets
CDP doesn't route.
CDP uses the default gateway
CDP never leaves the link.
The routers have proxy ARP turned on by default
Proxy ARP has nothing to do with CDP.

q.q: A CDP entry shows Capability R S I for neighbor CORE1. What kind of device is CORE1?
o: A Layer 3 switch
Right. R is router, S is switch, I is IGMP.
An IP phone
Phones show capability P.
A Layer 2 switch with no routing
R means it can route.
A host or server with no switching or routing
S means switching.

q.q: From R1, ping 10.3.3.1 (R3's LAN gateway) works. But PCs on R1's LAN 10.1.1.0/24 can't reach R3's LAN. An extended ping from R1 sourced from 10.1.1.1 fails. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: R3 has no route back to 10.1.1.0/24
Right. A normal ping uses R1's outgoing interface address, which R3 knows. Sourcing from the LAN shows the return path is missing.
R1's LAN interface is shut down
Then the extended ping couldn't use it as a source.
R3's LAN interface is down
The normal ping to 10.3.3.1 worked.
PCs on R1's LAN have the wrong DNS server
This is about IP reachability.

q.q: A traceroute from a PC to a server shows hops 1 and 2, then * * * on every later line. What does that tell you?
o: The problem is at or past hop 3
Right. Look at the device after hop 2 for a missing route, an ACL or a down link.
Hops 1 and 2 are down
They replied, so they're up.
The PC's DNS server failed
Traceroute by IP doesn't depend on DNS.
The server is fine, because traceroute often shows stars at the end
Stars on every line after hop 2 mean nothing beyond it answered.

q.q: Traceroute shows 10.0.12.2, 10.0.12.1, 10.0.12.2, 10.0.12.1 until it times out. What is happening?
o: A routing loop between two routers
Right. Packets bounce between the same two hops until the TTL runs out.
The destination is rate-limiting ICMP
Then later hops would just time out.
Spanning tree is blocking a port
STP issues are Layer 2. These are Layer 3 hops.
Normal load balancing
Load balancing doesn't send packets back and forth.

q.q: show ip interface brief shows Gi0/0/1 as 'up' in Status and 'down' in Protocol. What does this usually mean?
o: A Layer 2 problem, like keepalives
Right. Up/down points to a data link problem, not cabling.
The interface was shut down by an admin
That shows as administratively down.
The cable is unplugged
An unplugged cable shows down/down.
The interface is working normally
Working is up/up.

q.q: A ping from R1 returns U.U.U. What does this mean?
o: A router said unreachable
Right. U means a device reported the destination unreachable, often because it has no route.
Every reply came back fine
Success is shown as !.
Every request timed out with no reply at all
Timeouts show as periods.
The destination is busy
U isn't a busy signal.

q.q: A switch logs %SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF: Host 0050.56ab.1234 in vlan 10 is flapping between port Gi1/0/1 and port Gi1/0/2. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: A Layer 2 loop
Right. The same MAC showing up on two ports over and over usually means frames are looping.
A bad DHCP pool
DHCP doesn't move MACs between ports.
An OSPF neighbor down
OSPF is Layer 3.
A duplex mismatch
Duplex problems cause collisions, not MAC moves.

q.q: A PC never gets a DHCP address. You need to know whether its Discover even reaches the switch port. What is the BEST tool?
o: A packet capture on the port
Right. Capturing on the port shows whether the Discover arrives.
traceroute from the switch to the DHCP server
Traceroute tests a routed path. The PC has no address yet.
show ip route
Routing tables don't show DHCP traffic.
show cdp neighbors
CDP shows Cisco neighbors, not DHCP packets.

q.q: Three switches are in VLAN 1. Which one becomes the root bridge?
o: SW3
Right. The lowest bridge ID wins, and priority is compared before MAC. 28673 is lowest.
SW2
SW2 has the lowest MAC, but MAC only breaks ties between equal priorities.
SW1
SW1 has the default priority and a higher MAC than SW2.
None, because the priorities must match
Priorities don't need to match.
q.code:
SW1  priority 32769  MAC 0000.1111.1111
SW2  priority 32769  MAC 0000.0000.0001
SW3  priority 28673  MAC ffff.ffff.ffff

q.q: SW4 can reach the root two ways: Gi1/0/1, a 100 Mb/s link straight to the root, or Gi1/0/2, a 10 Gb/s link to SW5, which has a 10 Gb/s link to the root. Short-method costs: 100M = 19, 10G = 2. Which is SW4's root port?
o: Gi1/0/2, with a total cost of 4
Right. 2 + 2 = 4 beats 19. STP picks the lowest total path cost, not the fewest hops.
Gi1/0/1, because it connects straight to the root
Fewer hops doesn't matter. Its cost of 19 is higher.
Gi1/0/1, because its cost is lower at 2
The direct link is 100 Mb/s, which costs 19.
Neither, because both ports block
Every switch other than the root has one root port.

q.q: In Rapid PVST+, what is an alternate port?
o: A port with a backup path to the root, kept discarding
Right. It takes over quickly if the root port fails.
The port that leads to the root bridge
That's the root port.
The forwarding port on a segment, away from the root
That's a designated port.
A backup to another port on the same segment from the same switch
That's a backup port.

q.q: Which list shows the Rapid PVST+ (802.1w) port states?
o: Discarding, learning, forwarding
Right. RSTP folds blocking, listening and disabled into discarding.
Blocking, listening, learning, forwarding
Those are classic 802.1D states.
Down, init, 2-way, full
Those are OSPF neighbor states.
Active, standby, listen, speak
Those are HSRP states.

q.q: A user plugs a small switch into a PortFast access port that has BPDU guard. What happens?
o: The port goes err-disabled
Right. BPDU guard shuts edge ports that hear BPDUs, which stops loops.
The small switch becomes root
BPDU guard stops that by shutting the port.
The port changes to a trunk
BPDU guard doesn't change the port mode.
The BPDUs are quietly dropped and the port keeps forwarding
That's closer to what BPDU filter does.

q.q: A distribution switch has root guard on ports facing access switches. An access switch starts sending superior BPDUs. What happens?
o: It blocks as root-inconsistent
Right. Root guard keeps the root where you planned it.
The access switch becomes root
Root guard prevents exactly that.
The port goes err-disabled until an admin resets it
Root guard recovers by itself when the BPDUs stop.
The VLAN is deleted
STP never deletes VLANs.

q.q: A fiber link fails one way: SW2 stops getting BPDUs on its alternate port, though the link stays up. Which feature stops that port from moving to forwarding and making a loop?
o: Loop guard
Right. Loop guard puts the port in loop-inconsistent state instead of letting it become designated.
PortFast
PortFast speeds up edge ports. It would make things worse.
BPDU guard
BPDU guard acts when a BPDU arrives, not when they stop.
Storm control
Storm control limits traffic rates.

q.q: R1 has these routes. Where does it send a packet for 10.1.1.9?
o: Right. The longest prefix that matches wins: /24 beats /16 and /8, even with a higher AD and metric.
The static has a better AD, but AD only compares routes to the same prefix.
The /8 matches, but it's the least specific.
It load-balances across all three
Different prefixes aren't load-balanced.

q.q: R1 learns 192.168.50.0/24 from OSPF and also has a static route to the same prefix. Which one goes in the routing table?
o: The static route, AD 1
Right. For the same prefix, the lower administrative distance wins. Static is 1, OSPF 110.
The OSPF route, AD 110
110 is higher, so it loses.
Both, load-balanced
Different sources with different ADs aren't load-balanced.
Whichever arrived first
Arrival order doesn't decide.

q.q: What do the numbers in [110/20] mean in this route?
o: AD 110, metric 20
Right. AD comes first, then the protocol's metric. For OSPF, the metric is cost.
Metric 110, with a hop count of 20
OSPF doesn't use hop count.
Area 110, cost 20
Area numbers aren't shown in the brackets.
Priority 110, router ID 20
Neither belongs in the route brackets.

q.q: A router's table has no route for 8.8.8.8 except the one below. What happens to a packet for 8.8.8.8?
o: It's sent to 203.0.113.1 by default
Right. 0.0.0.0/0 matches anything when nothing more specific does.
It's dropped, because 8.8.8.8 isn't listed in the table
The default route catches it.
It's flooded out every interface
Routers don't flood unknown traffic.
It's sent back to the source
Routers don't do that.
q.code:
Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0
S*   0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1

q.q: In show ip route, what does a route with code L, such as 10.1.1.1/32, show?
o: The router's own address
Right. L is local: the exact address set on an interface.
A route learned by LLDP
LLDP doesn't put routes in the table.
A loopback network learned from an OSPF neighbor
Learned routes have protocol codes like O or S.
A floating static
Statics show as S.

q.q: R1 has two OSPF routes to 10.50.0.0/24, both cost 20, through different neighbors. What does it do?
o: Installs both and load-balances (ECMP)
Right. Equal-cost paths from the same protocol are installed together.
Keeps only the newest one
Equal routes are both kept.
Keeps the one with the lower next-hop IP
That isn't how ties are handled.
Drops both as a loop
Equal-cost paths aren't loops.

q.q: R1 has no default route and no route that matches 172.20.9.9. What does it do with a packet for that address?
o: Drops it, maybe with an ICMP unreachable
Right. With no match, the router can't forward it.
Sends it out its fastest interface
Routers don't guess.
Broadcasts it on every LAN
Routers don't broadcast unknown traffic.
Queues it until a matching route appears
Packets aren't stored waiting for routes.

q.q: R1 learns its default route from OSPF. You want a static default through a backup ISP that's used only if the OSPF route disappears. Which command?
o: Right. AD 200 is worse than OSPF's 110, so the static stays out until OSPF's route is gone.
With AD 1, the static would beat OSPF at once.
100 is better than 110, so it would take over right away.
ip default-gateway 198.51.100.1
That's for devices that don't route.

q.q: A floating static backup was added with AD 5, behind a primary OSPF route. What happens?
o: The static takes over at once
Right. A floating static needs an AD higher than the primary route's.
It works as a backup only
It would be preferred all the time.
The router rejects AD 5
AD 5 is valid. It's just wrong here.
OSPF raises its own AD so it stays preferred
Protocol ADs don't change by themselves.

q.q: You want R1 to reach one server, 10.5.5.5, through 10.0.0.2, while the rest of 10.5.5.0/24 goes elsewhere. Which route?
o: Right. A /32 host route matches only that address and beats the /24.
That moves the whole subnet.
That mask doesn't match the address as a host route.
That's a default route.

q.q: IPv6 static routes on R1 look right, but R1 won't forward any IPv6 traffic between interfaces. What is MOST likely missing?
o: ipv6 unicast-routing
Right. IOS doesn't route IPv6 until this global command is on.
ipv6 enable on every interface
Interfaces with global addresses already have IPv6.
ip routing
That's for IPv4.
An IPv6 default route on the PCs
Hosts learn gateways from RAs, and the router still won't forward.

q.q: You add ip route 10.9.9.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.9.2, but show ip route doesn't list it. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The next hop isn't reachable
Right. IOS won't install a static route whose next hop it can't reach.
Static routes only show up after the router reloads
Static routes appear right away.
The mask must be /32
/24 is fine for a network route.
OSPF hides static routes
OSPF doesn't hide statics.

q.q: An IPv6 static route uses a link-local next hop. What else must it include?
o: The outgoing interface
Right. Link-local addresses repeat on every link, so the router must know which one.
A /128 prefix
The destination prefix can be any size.
An AD of 1
AD 1 is already the default.
The keyword permanent at the end of the command
permanent keeps a route when an interface is down. It isn't required.

q.q: R1 has a static route to R2's LAN 10.2.2.0/24, and R2 has a default route to its ISP but no route to R1's LAN 10.1.1.0/24. PCs on R1's LAN ping R2's LAN. What happens?
o: Replies are lost via R2's ISP
Right. Routing works one direction at a time. R2 needs a route back to 10.1.1.0/24.
It works, because R1's route covers both ways
Each router routes on its own table.
R1 drops the requests
R1 has a route to 10.2.2.0/24.
R2 sends the replies back through R1 by default
R2 follows its default route to the ISP.

q.q: R1 and R2 share a link in area 0, but show ip ospf neighbor is empty. R1's hello interval is 10 and R2's is 5. What is the cause?
o: Hello and dead timers must match
Right. Mismatched timers mean the hellos are ignored.
The router IDs are different
Router IDs must be different.
The priorities are different
Priority affects DR election, not whether neighbors form.
R2 has a lower OSPF cost on that link
Cost doesn't stop neighbors from forming.

q.q: Two OSPF routers sit in EXSTART/EXCHANGE and never reach FULL. Routes don't swap. What should you check FIRST?
o: The interface MTU on both ends
Right. An MTU mismatch is the classic cause of being stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE.
The hello timers
Mismatched timers stop hellos before EXSTART.
The area IDs
An area mismatch stops the neighbor at the hello stage.
The DR priority on each router's interface
Priority doesn't cause this.

q.q: On a broadcast segment, R1 (priority 1, RID 1.1.1.1) is DR and R2 (priority 1, RID 2.2.2.2) is BDR. R3 joins with priority 200. What happens?
o: R1 stays DR, with no preemption
Right. A higher priority wins only at the next election, when the DR or BDR fails.
R3 takes over as DR at once
OSPF DR election doesn't preempt.
R3 becomes BDR at once, replacing R2 in that role
The BDR doesn't change either.
All three become DR
There's one DR per segment.

q.q: R1 has no router-id command, loopback 0 at 10.255.0.1, and physical interfaces at 192.168.1.1 and 172.16.0.1. What is its OSPF router ID?
o: Right. With no manual ID, OSPF picks the highest loopback address before any physical one.
That's the highest physical IP, but a loopback is preferred.
That's neither the highest nor a loopback.
OSPF picks an ID automatically.

q.q: Two routers are connected back to back over Ethernet with nothing else on the link. What does ip ospf network point-to-point on both ends do?
o: It skips the DR/BDR election
Right. A point-to-point link has only two routers, so no DR is needed.
It makes the link carry only OSPFv3 and IPv6 traffic
Network type has nothing to do with IPv6.
Turns off hellos
Hellos still keep the adjacency alive.
Puts the link in area 1
The area is set separately.

q.q: On a LAN with a DR, a BDR and two other routers, R3 shows R4 like this. Is there a problem?
o: No, that's normal between DROTHERs
Right. That's normal on a broadcast segment.
Yes, every neighbor must be FULL
Only DR and BDR adjacencies go FULL.
Yes, 2WAY means the MTU doesn't match on the link
MTU problems leave neighbors in EXSTART or EXCHANGE.
Yes, R4 has the wrong area
With the wrong area, R4 wouldn't show up at all.
q.code:
R3#show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID  Pri  State          Interface
4.4.4.4      1    2WAY/DROTHER   Gi0/0/0

q.q: An IPv6-only router runs OSPFv3 and won't start the process. It has no IPv4 addresses. What is missing?
o: A manual 32-bit router ID
Right. OSPFv3 still uses a 32-bit router ID. With no IPv4 address to borrow, you set it with router-id.
An IPv6 link-local address
Link-local addresses are created automatically.
An area 1 interface
Single-area OSPF can use area 0 only.
IPv4 routing
OSPFv3 doesn't need IPv4 routing.

q.q: Hosts in VLAN 10 use 10.10.10.1 as their gateway. Based on this output, which router forwards their traffic?
o: R1, the active router for virtual IP 10.10.10.1
Right. The active router answers for the virtual IP and its virtual MAC.
10.10.10.3, the standby router
The standby only takes over if R1 fails.
Both, load-balanced per packet
One HSRP group has one active router.
Neither, because 10.10.10.1 isn't on a real interface
The virtual IP is answered by the active router.
q.code:
R1#show standby brief
Interface Grp Pri P State   Active    Standby    Virtual IP
Vl10      10  110 P Active  local     10.10.10.3 10.10.10.1

q.q: R1 (priority 110) was HSRP active. It rebooted, and R2 (priority 100) took over. When R1 came back, R2 stayed active. Why?
o: Preempt isn't set on R1
Right. Without standby preempt, a higher-priority router won't take back the active role.
R1's priority is too high
Higher priority should win, but only with preempt.
HSRP never fails over
It just did.
R2 has the higher IP address, which always wins
IP breaks ties only when priorities are equal.

q.q: Two HSRP routers have priority 100, the default. R1's address is 10.1.1.2 and R2's is 10.1.1.3. With no preemption, both come up at the same time. Which becomes active?
o: R2, with the higher IP
Right. With equal priority, the highest interface IP wins.
R1, because the lower IP wins
Lower IP doesn't win in HSRP.
Both
Only one is active.
Neither, until a priority is set on one of them
Default priority 100 works.

q.q: A VRRP group uses virtual IP 10.20.20.1, which is also R1's real interface address. What is R1's role?
o: IP address owner, priority 255, normally master
Right. In VRRP, the router that owns the virtual IP gets priority 255.
Backup, because owners can't be master
Owners are always master when they're up.
Nothing, because VRRP can't use a real interface IP
VRRP allows it. HSRP doesn't.
Standby with priority 100
Standby is an HSRP term.

q.q: Hosts see a gateway MAC of 0000.0c07.ac0a. What does it tell you?
o: HSRP version 1, group 10
Right. HSRPv1 virtual MACs are 0000.0c07.acXX, with the group in hex (0a = 10).
VRRP group 10
VRRP uses 0000.5e00.01XX.
A Cisco router's burned-in MAC
This is a reserved virtual MAC.
HSRP version 2, group 172
HSRPv2 uses 0000.0c9f.fXXX.

q.q: show standby brief shows 'Active' on BOTH R1 and R2 for group 10. What is the MOST likely problem?
o: Hellos aren't getting through
Right. Each router thinks it's alone, so both go active.
Both routers have preempt
Preempt doesn't make both active.
The virtual IP is wrong on the hosts
Hosts don't affect HSRP state.
It's normal for HSRP version 2 with two routers
One active per group is the rule in every version.

q.q: R1 is HSRP active, but its WAN uplink just failed. Its LAN interface is still up. How do you make R2 take over?
o: Track the uplink, preempt on R2
Right. Tracking drops R1 below R2, and preempt lets R2 take the active role.
Turn off HSRP on R2
Then nothing can take over.
Change the virtual IP
Hosts would lose their gateway.
Raise R1's priority so it stays in control
That keeps R1 active.

q.q: Which local user command stores the password MOST securely on IOS?
o: username admin algorithm-type scrypt secret Str0ng!
Right. secret stores a strong one-way hash. Type 9 (scrypt) is the strongest choice here.
username admin privilege 15 password Str0ng!
password stores plain text, or weak type 7 with service password-encryption.
enable password Str0ng!
enable password isn't hashed, and it isn't a user account.
service password-encryption alone
This only applies reversible type 7 to existing passwords.

q.q: Why do many teams pick TACACS+ over RADIUS for admin logins to routers and switches?
o: Full encryption, per-command rules
Right. TACACS+ separates the three As and supports per-command authorization.
It uses UDP, so it's faster
TACACS+ uses TCP 49. RADIUS uses UDP.
It's the only one that works with Active Directory
Both can tie into directory services.
It encrypts only the password
That's RADIUS.

q.q: With this config, when does the router use its local user database?
o: Only when no TACACS+ server answers
Right. local is a fallback for when the servers can't be reached, not when they reject a login.
Every time, before trying TACACS+
The list is tried in order, so TACACS+ comes first.
When TACACS+ rejects the password
A reject is final. It doesn't fall through to local.
Never, because local can't be used with aaa new-model
local works fine in AAA lists.
q.code:
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local

q.q: Admins must log in to vty lines with local accounts, over SSH only. Which line config fits?
o: This config
Right. login local uses the username database, and transport input ssh blocks Telnet.
This config, but with transport input telnet ssh
That still allows cleartext Telnet.
This config, but with login instead of login local
login alone uses the line password, not user accounts.
This config, but on line console 0
The console isn't a remote vty line.
q.code:
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh

q.q: Why use SCP or SFTP instead of TFTP to back up router configs?
o: Encryption and a login
Right. TFTP sends files in clear text with no authentication.
They use UDP 69, which is faster
TFTP uses UDP 69. SCP and SFTP run over SSH on TCP 22.
TFTP can't copy files bigger than 1 KB
TFTP can copy configs and images.
SCP doesn't need SSH or keys on the router
SCP runs over SSH.

q.q: SSH to R1 works, but copying an image to R1 over SCP fails. Which command is MOST likely missing on R1?
o: ip scp server enable
Right. IOS needs this before it accepts incoming SCP copies.
crypto key generate rsa
SSH already works, so keys exist.
ip ssh version 1
Version 1 is weaker, not a requirement.
service tftp enable
That's for TFTP, not SCP.

q.q: Which command copies R1's running config to an SCP server at 10.1.1.50 as user netops?
o: copy running-config scp://netops@10.1.1.50/r1.cfg
Right. The URL holds the user, server and file name.
copy scp running-config 10.1.1.50
Source and destination are in the wrong format.
scp running-config netops 10.1.1.50
That isn't IOS syntax.
copy running-config tftp://10.1.1.50/r1.cfg
That uses TFTP, not SCP.

q.q: After copying a new IOS XE image to flash, how do you confirm the file wasn't damaged?
o: Run verify /md5 and compare hashes
Right. A matching hash shows the file arrived intact.
show version
That shows the running image, not the new file.
Run dir flash: and check the file's date and time
A date doesn't prove the file is whole.
Reload and see if it boots
That's risky and proves less.

q.q: All hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 should share the address of Gi0/0/1 to reach the internet. Which command, with ACL 1 matching the LAN?
o: ip nat inside source list 1 interface Gi0/0/1 overload
Right. overload turns on PAT, so many hosts share one address by port.
ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.0 203.0.113.1
Static NAT maps one address to one address.
ip nat outside source list 1 interface Gi0/0/1
This translates outside addresses, not inside hosts.
A pool alone doesn't translate, and these aren't public addresses.

q.q: In NAT terms, what is the inside global address?
o: The inside host's public address
Right. Inside local is the private address. Inside global is what it's translated to.
The private address set on the inside host
That's inside local.
The real address of an internet server
That's outside global.
The address of the inside hosts' default gateway
The gateway isn't a NAT address type.

q.q: PAT is set up, but show ip nat translations is empty and hosts can't reach the internet. The ACL and the overload command look right. What is MOST likely missing?
o: The inside/outside interface tags
Right. Without them, the router doesn't know which traffic to translate.
ip routing
Routers route IPv4 by default.
A static NAT entry for each inside host
PAT doesn't need static entries.
An ACL denying the LAN
A deny would stop translation.

q.q: An internal web server at 192.168.1.10 must always be reachable from the internet at 203.0.113.10. Which command?
o: ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10
Right. Static NAT gives a fixed one-to-one mapping in both directions.
ip nat inside source list 1 interface Gi0/0/1 overload
PAT doesn't give inbound access to a fixed host.
ip nat outside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10
That translates outside addresses.
ip helper-address 192.168.1.10
Helper is for DHCP relay.

q.q: Email for example.com isn't arriving. Which DNS record tells other mail servers where to deliver it?
o: MX
Right. MX records name the mail servers for a domain.
PTR
PTR maps an IP back to a name.
CNAME
CNAME is an alias for another name.
NS
NS names the domain's DNS servers.

q.q: An analyst has an IP address from a log and wants its host name. Which record does a reverse lookup use?
o: PTR
Right. PTR records map addresses to names.
A
A maps a name to an IPv4 address.
MX
MX is for mail delivery.
AAAA
AAAA maps a name to an IPv6 address.

q.q: www.example.com should always point wherever web01.example.com points, without updating two IPs. Which record?
o: A CNAME for www
Right. The alias follows web01's own records.
A second A record for www with the same IP
That's two IPs to keep in sync.
An MX record for www
MX is for mail.
A PTR record for web01
PTR is for reverse lookups.

q.q: IPv6-only clients can't reach app.example.com by name. nslookup shows only one record: app.example.com A 198.51.100.20. What is missing?
o: An AAAA record
Right. IPv6 clients need a AAAA record with the IPv6 address.
A PTR record
Reverse records don't help forward lookups.
An NS record for app
NS is about delegation.
An MX record
MX is for mail.

q.q: Two branch routers must link their LANs over the internet all the time, with no user software. Which VPN type fits?
o: Site-to-site IPsec
Right. Gateways build the tunnel, and hosts don't need clients.
Remote-access VPN
Remote access is for single users with a client.
GRE with no IPsec
GRE alone isn't encrypted.
SSL web portal only
That's for single users in a browser.

q.q: Why do site-to-site VPNs use ESP rather than AH?
o: ESP encrypts the data, AH doesn't
Right. AH only authenticates. It also breaks through NAT.
AH is faster and more secure
AH gives no confidentiality.
ESP doesn't need keys
ESP needs keys from IKE.
AH works better through NAT and firewalls
AH covers the IP header, so NAT breaks it.

q.q: In IPsec tunnel mode, what happens to the original IP packet?
o: It's encrypted inside a new packet
Right. That hides the inside addresses, which is why site-to-site VPNs use it.
Only the payload is encrypted, and the original header stays
That's transport mode.
The packet is sent in clear text
Tunnel mode with ESP encrypts it.
The packet is turned into a TCP stream on port 443
IPsec doesn't do that.

q.q: A remote user's VPN client sits behind a home NAT router. Which port does IPsec use with NAT traversal?
o: UDP 4500
Right. NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP 4500 so NAT devices can pass it.
TCP 443
That's typical for SSL VPNs.
UDP 69
That's TFTP.
TCP 22
That's SSH.

q.q: Where should a standard ACL usually be placed, and why?
o: Near the destination
Right. Placed near the source, it could block that source from everything.
Close to the source, because it matches ports
Standard ACLs don't match ports.
On every interface, in the inbound direction
That's rarely needed and causes trouble.
Only on the WAN interface
Placement depends on the traffic.

q.q: After this ACL is applied inbound on Gi0/0/0, what happens to SSH from 10.1.1.20 to 10.2.2.10?
o: It's dropped by the implicit deny
Right. SSH (TCP 22) matches no line, so the hidden deny any drops it.
It's allowed, because only Telnet is denied
Nothing permits port 22.
It's allowed by the port 80 line
SSH is port 22, not 80.
